title: Woodmoor Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Woodmoor wells have a 315 ft median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $21,800-$34,000.
h1: Woodmoor, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Woodmoor sits over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and the permitted wells mapped within 5 miles show a fairly consistent pattern: most completed wells are in the 300-to-600-foot range, with a median depth of 315 feet. Reported yields are stronger than many buyers expect, but depth, water level, and construction cost still vary from lot to lot.

This page uses Colorado DWR permit records for the Woodmoor area, including nearby Monument, Palmer Lake, and Gleneagle. Treat the figures as planning information, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. A driller still needs to review the lot, access, geology, nearby well records, and the intended household use.

sections.heading: Woodmoor well depth: plan for the Denver Basin
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth near Woodmoor is 315 feet. The middle half runs from 260 to 405 feet, which is the most useful range when reviewing a drilling bid. A quote based on a hole around the median may be reasonable, but the local records also reach the 90th percentile at 549 feet, with the deepest recorded well at 2,500 feet.

Depth mix matters here. Six percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, 28% are from 100 to 300 feet, 58% are from 300 to 600 feet, and 8% are deeper than 600 feet. Permits name the Dawson aquifer most often, followed by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers and the Denver aquifer. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 100% of the records.

sections.heading: What Woodmoor wells produce
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 13.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute: that group represents 82% of the records. Another 17% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield results are uncommon in this dataset, with 1% reporting 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 0% under 1 gallon per minute. That does not guarantee a strong well on a specific lot. The permit yield is a measured or reported result, not a promise of long-term supply. Ask how the well was tested and match storage and pump equipment to the home’s demand. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Woodmoor water levels and the long view
sections.html:
The median static water level is 120 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 89 to 165 feet. That figure helps with pump planning and gives a buyer a practical comparison point when reviewing neighboring wells. It is not the same as total well depth: a well can continue substantially below the standing water level.

The decade figures do not show a steady downward trend. The median was 135 feet below surface in the 1970s, 125 in the 1980s, 121 in the 1990s, 130 in the 2000s, 110 in the 2010s, and 125 in the 2020s. The record is better described as fluctuating than as a consistent decline. Confirm current conditions with nearby wells and a driller before relying on a historical median.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Woodmoor, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity expanded substantially after the early records. The DWR file shows 34 permits from the 1950s, 55 from the 1960s, 590 from the 1970s, 845 from the 1980s, 1,451 from the 1990s, 1,021 from the 2000s, 675 from the 2010s, and 534 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the area is 2025.

In the recorded drilling history, Fletcher Drilling, associated with Fletcher, Thomas, appears on 1,603 wells. Kunau Drilling LLC, associated with Kunau, Timothy R., appears on 1,068. Hamacher Well Works Inc., associated with Hamacher, Alan Ray, appears on 579. These records show who has worked nearby, but they are not a recommendation or a substitute for checking current licensing, insurance, availability, and references.

sections.heading: Woodmoor well drilling cost at the median depth
sections.html:
The cost model for Woodmoor’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock uses a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 315-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $15,800 to $22,000. That is only the drilling portion of the project.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $21,800 to $34,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, longer utility runs, casing or grout requirements, and site conditions can move the actual bid outside that planning range. When comparing proposals, confirm what is included, the assumed depth, casing and grout, pump capacity, testing, permits, trenching, electrical work, and restoration.

sections.heading: Woodmoor risks to check before closing or building
sections.html:
Water quality deserves its own review. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 25 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped locations do not prove contamination at a particular well, but they are a reason to obtain a current laboratory water test and review the well’s construction and history.

Also investigate low yield, dry-hole risk, and the distance between the well, septic system, and proposed building. Casing and grout protect the well from surface entry, but condition and installation matter. Domestic or household use represents 84% of the recorded use mix. Stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells make up other portions, so verify that an existing permit matches your intended use. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses.

sections.heading: Buying or building a Woodmoor lot
sections.html:
Before making an offer, pull the nearby DWR permits and compare total depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer name, use, and construction details. The records within 5 miles provide a useful starting point, especially when a parcel has no well yet. Monument, Palmer Lake, Gleneagle, and the Air Force Academy can provide additional local context, but conditions can change across short distances.

For a new build, have a driller inspect access and identify a practical well location before finalizing the house site. Price the well together with septic, driveway, trenching, electrical service, storage, and testing. Confirm legal water use before construction, particularly if the property is in an area requiring augmentation. A strong neighboring yield is encouraging, but it is not a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Woodmoor, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Woodmoor is 315 feet. The middle half runs from 260 to 405 feet, while 58% of reported wells are 300 to 600 feet deep. Some are much deeper: the 90th percentile is 549 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 2,500 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Woodmoor?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 315-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $15,800 to $22,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $21,800 to $34,000. Actual bids depend on access, depth, construction, and utility distances.

faq.q: How much water do Woodmoor wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 11.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 13.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-two percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 17% report more than 15. A neighboring result is useful evidence, but it does not guarantee the same yield on your parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Woodmoor?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 25 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Have the well water tested by a qualified laboratory, review construction records, and check the well’s location relative to possible sources before drinking it.

faq.q: Is the Woodmoor water table dropping?
faq.a: The recorded decade medians do not show a steady decline. Static water levels were 135 feet below surface in the 1970s, 125 in the 1980s, 121 in the 1990s, 130 in the 2000s, 110 in the 2010s, and 125 in the 2020s. The pattern fluctuates, so current neighboring-well data remains important for a purchase or new build.
